Heatcraft (Bohn/Larkin):
Heatcraft Refrigeration is the biggest name in walk-in cooler and freezer refrigeration in North America — its equipment sells under the Bohn and Larkin brands (plus Climate Control and Chandler), so if your walk-in's evaporator says Bohn or Larkin on it, Heatcraft's controllers are what's talking to you. Current unit coolers ship with the intelliGen controller: an OLED display with a colored light bar where red plus an AL code is an alarm (AL01 high box temperature, AL06 door open), yellow plus an ER code is an error — usually a failed sensor — and IN codes are informational. Units running the newer A2L refrigerants add leak-detection alarms (AL12, ER32) that are evacuate-ventilate-and-call events, not troubleshooting exercises.

The previous generation, Beacon II, uses A1–A4 alarms and E1–E9 errors, several of which pump the system down and keep it off until the failed sensor is replaced — which makes an E-code on a Beacon II an urgent call, because your product is warming while it waits. Find your exact code below for the documented meaning, the checks facility staff can safely make, and the point where the clock says call now.
KE2 Therm:
KE2 Therm's Evaporator Efficiency controller is fitted to thousands of walk-ins — sometimes from the factory, often as a retrofit that pays for itself in defrost energy savings. It skips cryptic codes entirely and scrolls named alarms across its display: HIGH AIR TEMP, DOOR SWITCH, EXCESS DEFROST, LOW SUPERHEAT. The LED color is your severity gauge — yellow means the system is still running and you have time to diagnose; a red critical alarm like PRESSURE SENSOR means the controller shut refrigeration down to protect the compressor, and box temperature is now rising on the clock.

Two KE2-specific things worth knowing. First, the VARIABLES menu turns sensor alarms into instant diagnosis: a reading of -87 means the sensor is open or unplugged, 180+ means it's shorted. Second, several KE2 alarms are really system diagnoses — LOW SUPERHEAT most commonly means the compressor never started (frequently a low-pressure control that was never field-set, which shows up as the weather cools each fall). Find your exact alarm below for what it means, what to check, and when to call.
Dixell (Emerson):
The small Dixell XR-series controller — now an Emerson/Copeland product — is probably the most common digital thermostat on walk-in coolers in America. Box builders including Norlake and Kolpak have shipped it for years, so the two-letter codes on that little display are the fault language of a huge share of walk-ins. The vocabulary is short: P1 through P4 are probe (sensor) failures, HA and LA are high and low temperature alarms, HA2/LA2 condenser temperature alarms, dA the door alarm, EA an external device alarm — and CA is the serious one, meaning a critical input tripped and the controller switched every output off.

The most useful thing to know about a Dixell is what it does during a probe failure: on P1 the controller keeps the box running on timed compressor cycles instead of actual temperature, so the cooler limps along while quietly needing a sensor. And the code that generates the most confused service calls isn't a fault at all — OF or PoF just means the keypad is locked (hold the up and down arrows for three seconds). Find your code below for the documented meaning and next steps.
Norlake:
Norlake is one of the major American walk-in box manufacturers, and its factory control option is a programmable control panel built on Carel hardware that skips code numbers entirely — it scrolls plain-text alarms: DOOR AJAR ALARM, ROOM TEMP HIGH ALARM, AIR FLOW LOSS, ROOM TEMPERATURE SENSOR FAILURE. Read them literally, and use the ALARM button to view and silence while you investigate. The status line is the part most people miss: it reports fallback modes like USING PROD SENSOR or SENSOR FAIL MODE that tell you the panel is running your box on backup logic — cooling continues, but the failed sensor needs a prompt service visit, not a shrug.

Worth knowing: many Norlake (and Kolpak) walk-ins ship with the Dixell controller covered elsewhere on this site instead of the programmable panel — check what your display actually looks like. If it shows two-letter codes like P1 or HA, you want the Dixell pages; if it scrolls sentences, you're in the right place below.
Danfoss:
Danfoss electronic controllers run an enormous share of commercial refrigeration, and several of its families end up on walk-in coolers and their condensing units: the ERC 211/213/214 controllers found on cabinets and walk-in control panels, the EKC 202 and AK-CC 210/250 case and room controllers, and the Optyma Plus controller mounted on Danfoss condensing units that serve walk-ins. The code language is consistent across them: E-codes are sensor and electronics errors (E29 is the air sensor, E27 the defrost sensor), A-codes are alarms — temperature (A01/A02 or A1/A2), door (A04/A4), voltage protection (A99/AA1), and the condenser pair worth memorizing: A61 warns the condenser is running hot, A80 is the blocked-condenser lockout that requires a manual reset after you clean the coil.

Some AK-CC models add HACCP logging (A60) that timestamps food-safety excursions. Find your controller family and exact code below for the documented meaning, the safe checks, and when it's a service call.
Carel:
Carel controllers are fitted by walk-in and refrigeration OEMs worldwide — most commonly the ir33 / ir33+ family and the smaller PJ Easy (PJEZ), the compact digital thermostats you'll find running boxes from many different builders. Their code language is compact: E-codes are probe faults (E0 room probe, E1 defrost probe, E2 condenser probe), HI and LO are the temperature alarms, dor/dOR the door alarm, Ed/Ed1 means a defrost timed out before clearing the coil, and the condenser pair — lowercase cht as the dirty-condenser early warning, uppercase CHt as the hard alarm — is the difference between a cleaning reminder and a compressor at risk. A code that fools everyone: dEF or dF isn't a fault at all, just the display's way of saying a defrost is running.

Carel controllers on HACCP-equipped installs also log HA/HF temperature-excursion events. Find your exact code below for the documented meaning, safe checks, and the technician threshold.
